questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on his right hand with raised, indurated, rolled edges. The base shows granulation tissue and regional lymph nodes are enlarged but non-tender. Smear from the ulcer shows acid-fast bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Buruli ulcer caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans presents as a painless ulcer with undermined edges. It is AFB positive and common in tropical farming communities. TB chancre is usually associated with regional lymphadenopathy but typically presents differently. The painless nature and AFB positivity point strongly to M. ulcerans.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompetent patient presents with annular scaly plaques on the trunk. KOH preparation shows hyphae and arthrospores. Cultures grow a slow-growing colony with powdery texture after 3 weeks at 37°C. Wood's lamp examination is negative. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Trichophyton rubrum is the most common cause of tinea corporis in adults. It is a slow-growing dermatophyte that does not fluoresce under Wood's lamp. T. tonsurans causes most tinea capitis cases in the US. M. canis fluoresces green under Wood's lamp. E. floccosum affects skin and nails but not hair.

questions.q: A 22-year-old sexually active male presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the penile shaft, associated with inguinal lymphadenopathy and fever. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. The first episode was 2 weeks ago. Which antiviral drug should be used for episodic treatment?
questions.exp: Valacyclovir 500mg BD for 3 days is the preferred short-course episodic therapy for recurrent genital herpes per current CDC guidelines. It offers equivalent efficacy with improved bioavailability compared to acyclovir. Acyclovir 400mg TDS for 5 days is also acceptable but requires longer duration.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male from a leprosy-endemic area presents with a single hypopigmented patch with well-defined margins, decreased sensation, and no hair within the patch. Slit-skin smear is negative. Nerve thickening is absent. What is the classification of this patient's leprosy?
questions.exp: Polar tuberculoid (TT) leprosy presents with a single, well-defined hypopigmented patch with complete loss of sensation, anhidrosis, and alopecia within the patch. Slit-skin smear is negative (paucibacillary). Indeterminate leprosy has ill-defined borders with partial sensory loss. BT has 2-5 lesions. BL has numerous lesions with satellite papules.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and arthritis for 3 months. Lab shows ANA positive (1:320), anti-dsDNA positive, low C3 and C4. She is started on hydroxychloroquine. After 2 months, what monitoring is most essential?
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine can cause irreversible retinal toxicity (bull's eye maculopathy) due to accumulation in retinal pigment epithelium. Baseline ophthalmological examination before starting and annual reviews after 5 years (or earlier in high-risk patients) are mandatory. This is the most feared and irreversible side effect.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male on penicillamine for rheumatoid arthritis develops tense blisters on the abdomen and thighs with positive Nikolsky sign. Direct immunofluorescence shows IgG and C3 deposits at the epidermal cell surface in a 'fishnet' pattern. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Drug-induced pemphigus can be triggered by penicillamine, captopril, and other thiol-containing drugs. The clinical and immunofluorescence pattern mimics pemphigus vulgaris with positive Nikolsky sign and intercellular IgG deposits. However, drug cessation often leads to resolution, unlike true pemphigus vulgaris. D-penicillamine is the most common culprit.

questions.q: A 68-year-old male presents with a pearly nodule with telangiectasia on the nose, present for 8 months. It has a central depression and occasional bleeding. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels. Excision biopsy shows palisading nuclei at the periphery of tumor islands. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.exp: This is a basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose (H-zone/high-risk area). Mohs micrographic surgery is the treatment of choice for BCCs in high-risk locations (nose, periorbital, ears) as it offers the highest cure rate with maximal tissue preservation by examining 100% of margins intraoperatively.

questions.q: A 32-year-old pregnant woman (28 weeks) presents with intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques on the abdomen, initially within striae gravidarum, sparing the umbilicus. Direct immunofluorescence is negative. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP)
questions.exp: PUPPP (now called polymorphic eruption of pregnancy) characteristically begins within striae distensae, spares the umbilicus, and direct immunofluorescence is negative. It is benign with no fetal risk. Pemphigoid gestationis involves the umbilicus, has positive DIF (C3 at BMZ), and carries fetal risk. Cholestasis presents with pruritus without primary skin lesions.

questions.q: A 19-year-old male presents with painful genital ulcers that are soft, ragged, with undermined edges and a necrotic base. No vesicles are seen. Gram stain of the exudate shows 'school of fish' arrangement of gram-negative rods. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: This is chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. The classic 'school of fish' Gram stain pattern is pathognomonic. Azithromycin 1g single dose is the preferred CDC-recommended treatment. Ciprofloxacin 500mg BD for 3 days is an alternative. Benzathine penicillin is used for syphilis. The soft, painful, undermined ulcer distinguishes it from syphilitic chancre.

questions.q: A 45-year-old female with longstanding psoriasis develops swollen, painful joints of her fingers and toes with sausage-shaped digits. X-ray shows 'pencil-in-cup' deformity. What type of psoriatic arthritis does she have?
questions.exp: Arthritis mutilans is the most severe and destructive form of psoriatic arthritis, characterized by osteolysis of phalanges leading to the classic 'pencil-in-cup' deformity on X-ray and 'opera glass' hands clinically. Dactylitis (sausage digits) can occur in multiple subtypes. The X-ray finding of pencil-in-cup is pathognomonic for arthritis mutilans.

questions.q: A 16-year-old presents with comedones, papules, and pustules on the face. Parents are concerned about starting isotretinoin. Which of the following is a MANDATORY requirement before initiating isotretinoin in a female patient?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (Category X). Two negative pregnancy tests (one at baseline, one at day 2-3 of next menstrual period) are mandatory before initiating treatment in females of childbearing potential. This is part of the iPLEDGE program in the US and similar REMS programs globally. Contraception must continue 1 month after stopping.

questions.q: A 30-year-old healthcare worker presents with vesicular eruption on the fingers following contact with a patient who had herpes labialis. The lesions are extremely painful with associated lymphadenopathy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Herpetic whitlow is HSV-1 or HSV-2 infection of the finger/periungual area, common in healthcare workers and young children. It presents with painful vesicles, erythema, and regional lymphadenopathy. It is an occupational hazard for dental and medical workers. Treatment is with acyclovir. It must not be incised as this can spread infection.

questions.q: A biopsy from a hypopigmented patch in a leprosy patient shows dermal granulomas with lymphocytes arranged in a 'mantle' around them, reaching up to the sub-epidermal zone, with no bacilli. Fite-Faraco stain is negative. This corresponds to which Ridley-Jopling classification?
questions.exp: Polar tuberculoid (TT) leprosy histologically shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells, lymphocytic mantle, involvement of the sub-epidermal zone (Grenz zone is absent), and no bacilli on Fite-Faraco stain. The granulomas may erode the epidermis. BT has similar but less well-formed granulomas and the sub-epidermal zone is preserved.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of urticaria and angioedema without itching, particularly involving the face, hands, and GI tract. Family history is positive. C4 is very low even between attacks. What is the pathophysiology?
opts: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency leading to bradykinin excess
Acquired C1q deficiency due to malignancy
questions.exp: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is caused by C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency. Without C1-INH, uncontrolled activation of the complement and contact pathways leads to bradykinin accumulation, which increases vascular permeability. It is characteristically non-pruritic, not responsive to antihistamines, and C4 is persistently low. Icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist) is used for acute attacks.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male presents with well-demarcated, silvery scaly plaques on the elbows, knees, and scalp with nail pitting. He requests narrowband UVB phototherapy. Which of the following is a contraindication to this treatment?
opts: History of basal cell carcinoma 5 years ago
questions.exp: Lupus erythematosus is an absolute contraindication to phototherapy as UV radiation can trigger or exacerbate the disease (photosensitivity is a cardinal feature of SLE). History of NMSC is a relative contraindication. Pregnancy is not a contraindication to narrowband UVB (it is actually preferred in pregnancy). Renal impairment does not contraindicate phototherapy.

questions.q: A 72-year-old male develops tense bullae on flexural areas with no mucosal involvement. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. ELISA confirms antibodies against BP180 and BP230. What cells primarily mediate the blister formation?
questions.exp: In bullous pemphigoid, autoantibodies against BP180 (type XVII collagen) activate complement and recruit eosinophils and neutrophils to the BMZ. These cells release proteases (MMP-9, neutrophil elastase) that cleave laminin and type XVII collagen, causing subepidermal blister formation. Eosinophilia is a characteristic finding in peripheral blood and blister fluid.

questions.q: A 38-year-old male with HIV (CD4 count 180 cells/μL) presents with large ulcerated nodules on his lower extremities. Biopsy shows proliferating spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells. What is the aetiological agent?
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8/KSHV). It is an AIDS-defining illness seen when CD4 count falls below 200 cells/μL. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular channels, and extravasated RBCs with hemosiderin deposits. Treatment includes HAART (which may cause immune reconstitution), liposomal doxorubicin for disseminated disease.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with intensely itchy, purple, polygonal, flat-topped papules on the flexor surface of the wrists with Wickham's striae visible. Mucosa shows lacy white network. What is the pathognomonic histological feature?
opts: Saw-toothing of rete ridges with band-like lymphocytic infiltrate and colloid bodies
questions.exp: Lichen planus histologically shows hyperkeratosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, irregular acanthosis with saw-tooth rete ridges, a dense band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ that obscures it, and colloid (Civatte/hyaline) bodies (necrotic keratinocytes). The 4 P's: Purple, Polygonal, Pruritic, Papules. DIF shows shaggy fibrin at the DEJ.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male construction worker presents with a hyperpigmented, hyperkeratotic plaque on the dorsum of his hand with areas of central clearing. The lesion has been present for 2 years. Dermoscopy shows clustered brown globules. Biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal dysplasia. What is this pre-malignant lesion?
opts: Bowen's disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ)
questions.exp: Bowen's disease is SCC in situ presenting as a slowly expanding erythematous or hyperkeratotic plaque. Histologically, there is full-thickness epidermal dysplasia with mitoses, dyskeratotic cells, and parakeratosis, with an intact basement membrane. Erythroplasia of Queyrat is SCC in situ on the glans penis. Actinic keratosis shows partial-thickness dysplasia.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male nurse presents after needlestick injury from an HBsAg-positive patient. He received full hepatitis B vaccination 5 years ago. His anti-HBs titer today is 8 mIU/mL. What is the appropriate post-exposure management?
opts: No treatment needed as he is vaccinated
questions.exp: Anti-HBs titer <10 mIU/mL indicates non-protective immunity despite prior vaccination (non-responder). After needlestick from HBsAg-positive source, a non-responder should receive HBIG (0.06 mL/kg IM) immediately plus revaccination series. HBIG provides passive immunity while the new vaccine series attempts to generate active immunity.

questions.q: A 60-year-old female on long-term methotrexate for psoriasis develops mucositis and cytopenias. Her folic acid supplementation was recently stopped. What is the mechanism of methotrexate toxicity in this scenario?
opts: Inhibition of purine synthesis via DHFR inhibition leading to folate deficiency
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), preventing conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate. This depletes folate cofactors needed for purine and thymidylate synthesis, impairing rapidly dividing cells (mucosa, bone marrow). Folic acid supplementation reduces non-immunological side effects without significantly compromising anti-inflammatory efficacy. Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescues in acute toxicity.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a hypopigmented macule on the cheek with absolute anesthesia. The regional auricular nerve is thickened and tender. Slit-skin smear shows a Bacterial Index (BI) of 3+. What MDT regimen should this patient receive?
opts: PB-MDT: Rifampicin 600mg monthly + Dapsone 100mg daily for 6 months
MB-MDT: Rifampicin 600mg monthly + Clofazimine 300mg monthly + 50mg daily + Dapsone 100mg daily for 12 months
questions.exp: A BI of 3+ classifies this as multibacillary (MB) leprosy. WHO MB-MDT consists of Rifampicin 600mg monthly (supervised) + Clofazimine 300mg monthly (supervised) + 50mg daily (unsupervised) + Dapsone 100mg daily (unsupervised) for 12 months. PB-MDT is for paucibacillary disease. ROM regimen is for single-lesion PB leprosy only.

questions.q: A 35-year-old female presents with diffuse non-scarring alopecia, widening of the central part, and positive hair pull test. Trichoscopy shows peripilar sign (brown halos around follicular ostia) and yellow dots. Serum ferritin is 8 ng/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium presents as diffuse hair shedding with positive pull test (more than 10% telogen hairs). The peripilar sign on trichoscopy represents perifollicular inflammation. Iron deficiency (ferritin <70 ng/mL) is a major trigger. FPHL shows miniaturization on trichoscopy. Alopecia areata shows exclamation mark hairs and cadaverized hairs (black dots). Treatment includes iron supplementation.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with a 2-week history of copper-colored maculopapular rash on the palms and soles, generalized lymphadenopathy, and mucous patches in the mouth. RPR is reactive 1:64. What stage of syphilis is this?
questions.exp: Secondary syphilis typically occurs 4-8 weeks after the primary chancre (which may have healed). Classic features include the 'great imitator' rash involving palms and soles (copper/ham-colored), generalized lymphadenopathy, mucous patches, condylomata lata, and systemic symptoms. High RPR titers confirm active infection. Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM x1 is first-line treatment.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, skin tightening involving the forearms and face, telangiectasias, and calcinosis cutis. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. What systemic complication is she most at risk for?
questions.exp: This is limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc, CREST syndrome). Anti-centromere antibody is associated with lcSSc. The most serious complication in lcSSc is pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), occurring in 10-15% of patients, which can be fatal. Scleroderma renal crisis (with anti-RNA polymerase III antibody) is more associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a painless verrucous plaque on his right lower leg of 2 years duration, following a minor injury while gardening. Culture shows olive-brown muriform (sclerotic) cells. Biopsy of the lesion confirms the medlar body appearance. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous (black) fungi (Fonsecaea pedrosoi most common). The pathognomonic finding is 'medlar bodies' (copper-colored, round, thick-walled muriform cells with internal septation) in tissue. The typical presentation is verrucous plaques on the lower extremities following traumatic inoculation. Mycetoma has grains; sporotrichosis has sporotrichoid spread.

questions.q: A 33-year-old male presents with painful erosions and flaccid blisters involving the oral mucosa and trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular 'chicken-wire' IgG deposition in the epidermis. Anti-desmoglein 3 antibody is markedly elevated. What is the first-line treatment?
opts: Oral prednisolone 1-1.5 mg/kg/day with azathioprine as steroid-sparing agent
Rituximab 1000mg IV two doses 2 weeks apart
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris treatment: systemic corticosteroids remain the cornerstone, usually prednisolone 1-1.5 mg/kg/day. Steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine 2-3 mg/kg/day, mycophenolate mofetil 2g/day) are added early to reduce cumulative steroid dose. Rituximab is now increasingly used as a first-line or early second-line agent in moderate-severe disease per recent evidence, but traditional practice uses steroids + adjuvant first.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with flesh-colored papules on the penile shaft, some with a central depression. HIV test is negative. The lesions have been increasing in number for 3 months. Dermoscopy shows central pore with white/yellow amorphous material and peripheral crown vessels. What is the treatment of choice for extensive lesions?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum caused by poxvirus presents with flesh-colored umbilicated papules. For extensive lesions in adults, cryotherapy is the preferred office-based treatment. Topical imiquimod is an alternative for multiple lesions. Podophyllin is used for genital warts (HPV), not molluscum. Physical destruction methods (curettage, cryotherapy) are most effective for rapid clearance.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with recurrent crops of erythematous annular lesions with a dusky center appearing during each episode of herpes labialis. The lesions resolve without scarring. Skin biopsy shows epidermal necrosis and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. What is the pathomechanism?
opts: Type I hypersensitivity reaction to HSV antigens
HSV antigen-triggered CD4+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity targeting HSV-infected keratinocytes
Immune complex deposition in dermal vessels
Direct HSV infection of skin at distant sites
questions.exp: Herpes-associated erythema multiforme (EM minor) is a CD4+ T cell-mediated hypersensitivity (type IV/delayed) reaction triggered by HSV antigens. HSV DNA fragments are carried by PBMC to skin where they are expressed in keratinocytes; HSV-specific CD4+ T cells then mediate cytotoxic attack on HSV-antigen-expressing keratinocytes, causing the characteristic targetoid lesions.

questions.q: During a Mohs surgery on a cheek BCC, the surgeon maps the removed layer and processes it for frozen section. All margins show tumor cells except the deep margin at 6 o'clock. The surgeon re-excises tissue from the 6 o'clock position only. What is the main advantage of Mohs surgery over traditional wide local excision?
opts: Complete margin assessment with maximum tissue conservation
Lower recurrence rate due to deeper excision
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery processes tissue so that 100% of the peripheral and deep surgical margin can be examined microscopically (en face sections covering the entire margin). This allows precise mapping of tumor extensions and targeted re-excision of only tumor-positive areas, maximizing cure rates while conserving normal tissue — critical in cosmetically and functionally sensitive areas.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl presents with well-defined brown patches with darker freckle-like spots within them on the trunk, present since birth. She also has bilateral axillary freckling and 7 café-au-lait spots >1.5 cm. Her ophthalmologist finds Lisch nodules. What complication requires most urgent monitoring?
questions.exp: This is Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Optic pathway glioma occurs in 15-20% of NF1 patients, usually in the first 6 years of life, and can cause vision loss if untreated. MRI brain surveillance is recommended. While malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNST) are a feared complication, optic glioma is more common and time-sensitive in pediatric patients.
